title: Customer priority briefing: latency surge response and customer action guide
content:
Purpose
This note is a customer-ready briefing and short post-incident summary template that CS can adapt for customers affected by the 2029-06-14 latency surge. It bundles a short status-page-ready blurb, a more detailed technical summary for partner teams, recommended immediate actions customers can take, and the proposed follow-up messaging cadence. Use the snippets below as-is or with light editing for tone.

Executive summary (one-line for status page)
We experienced a region-wide increase in request latency affecting text-generation and streaming responses in us-west-2 between 2029-06-14 03:10 and 2029-06-14 05:40 UTC; service remained available but at elevated latency for some tenants. Full remediation steps and root-cause analysis are in progress.

Short customer-facing status (200–300 words)
What happened: Between 03:10–05:40 UTC on 2029-06-14, a traffic pattern mismatch combined with an autoscaling race condition and a gradual KV-cache evictions spike led to higher-than-normal per-request latencies for a subset of requests that required large prefix context (>8k tokens). Some streaming sessions also exhibited delayed first-token times. No data loss or unauthorized access was observed.
Who was affected: Customers routing to our us-west-2 serving pool with workloads that have long prefix contexts or sustained bursts experienced slowdowns. Most embed/short-text workloads were unaffected.
What we did: We applied a multi-step mitigation: (1) disabled the aggressive autoscaling policy for the affected node pool, (2) forced a controlled warm-up redeploy to stabilize node-to-node cache affinity, (3) enabled a conservative model-fallback knob that routed long-prefix requests to the compatible quantized variant for latency-critical tiers, and (4) repaired a stale KV cache index. These actions reduced median P95 latency to within SLA by 05:10 UTC and completed recovery by 05:40 UTC.
Customer action checklist (recommended, ordered)
1) Short-term: implement exponential retry/backoff (initial 100ms, max 2s) and use idempotency keys for high-throughput request flows to avoid duplicate inference work.
2) Pin a stable model variant: if you depend on consistent latency, pin requests to the standard (non-experimental) model version via the model_version parameter in the SDK.
3) Prefer streaming with small initial chunk sizes: split very large prompts into prefix + streaming continuation when possible to reduce first-token delays.
4) Fallback handling: add a client-side permissive fallback to a shorter-context prompt or reduced max_tokens for latency-sensitive endpoints.
5) Observability: enable per-request timing headers and send a short sample of slow request metadata to support@redwood.ai if you see repeat problems.

Technical timeline (short)
- 2029-06-14 03:05 UTC: Monitoring alerts for P99 latency in us-west-2.
- 03:10 UTC: Incident declared, SRE+Serving runtime teams paged.
- 03:25 UTC: Correlation of alerts to increased KV eviction metrics and rapid scaling events.
- 03:40 UTC: First mitigation (disable aggressive autoscaler) applied; partial improvement noted.
- 04:05 UTC: Rolling controlled redeploy (warm-up affinity) started for affected pool.
- 05:10 UTC: Model-fallback routing enabled for latency tiers; P95 returned near SLA.
- 05:40 UTC: All recovery monitors green; incident moved to post-incident analysis.

Root cause summary (preview for customers)
Preliminary analysis indicates a compound failure: a newly introduced autoscaling heuristic reacted to a short-lived traffic burst by scaling down and then up rapidly, which caused mismatched KV-cache population across nodes. That mismatch increased cold-KV lookups for long-prefix requests, which in turn amplified tail latency. A configuration bug in a rollout of a kernel-selection optimizer made these lookups more expensive for a particular family of model variants.

What we are doing long-term
- Reverting the autoscaling heuristic change and replacing it with a stepwise scale policy with cooldown.
- Adding KV-cache reconciliation across node restarts to prevent asymmetric cold starts.
- Harden kernel-selection rollout: staged canary with latency-shadowing and abort on regressions.
- Expanding per-tenant routing telemetry and adding automated early-fallback triggers for long-prefix requests.

Suggested customer-facing postmortem (concise, 3–5 paragraphs)
Lead-in: We know any degradation is disruptive — thank you for your patience. This note summarizes our findings and the actions we’ve taken.
What happened: A combination of an autoscaling policy change and an unintended performance regression in a kernel-selection optimizer led to mismatched cache populations during a burst. This produced elevated latencies for long-context generation in us-west-2.
Impact: Affected customers saw increased P95/P99 latency for requests that used >8k token prefixes. Throughput and authentication were unaffected; no customer data was exposed.
Remediation & next steps: We restored stable autoscaling, rolled a targeted fix for KV-cache reconciliation, and introduced guardrails for kernel-selection rollouts. We will publish a full technical postmortem with timeline and remediation artifacts in 7 business days.

Suggested status page entries (two-staged)
- Immediate short: "Investigating latency increases affecting long-context generation in us-west-2. Service remains available; some customers may see elevated response times."
- Update when resolved: "Resolved — we mitigated the root cause and restored normal latency. A full post-incident summary will be available soon."

Suggested subject lines for customer emails
- "Update: Reduced latency restored for long-context generation (us-west-2)"
- "Incident summary and recommended actions: us-west-2 latency event"

FAQ snippets for pinning customers
Q: Was my data exposed?
A: No — this was a performance incident; there is no evidence of data leakage or unauthorized access.
Q: Will you compensate for SLA misses?
A: We will review tenant impact and follow standard SLA exception process; CS will reach out to any customers with measurable SLA violations.
Q: How can I reduce my exposure to similar events?
A: Implement the short-term checklist above, avoid relying on experimental model variants without pinning, and consider a Dedicated pool for strict latency SLOs.

Operational notes for CS engineers (quick copy/paste for support threads)
- Please ask customers to provide request IDs and sample timestamps for any slow calls.
- If customers are on streaming sessions and see delayed first-token, advise a small prompt split as a workaround.
- For enterprise customers: offer a conversation with Solutions Eng to discuss pinning Dedicated capacity or regional routing.

Next steps (internal)
- Finalize full postmortem, publish in 7 business days.
- Proactively reach out to customers who exceeded SLA thresholds.
- Track progress on autoscaling and KV-cache fixes with engineering; update customers when mitigations are merged and deployed.

Contact
Customer Success escalation: cs-escalations@redwood.ai
Incident lead: Meera Patel (meera@redwood.ai)
SRE on-call: slo-oncall@redwood.ai

End of briefing. Replace the prose with customer-specific details as needed before sending.
